# Coupled distal quantile deformation: exact laws and a genuine cap obstruction
It is distinct from independent fiber changes and from the archived
disjoint exposed-vertex removed-mass construction. It provides no
unconditional descent sign at a below-OC minimum.

## 1. Setting, exact quantiles, and a necessary plateau qualification

Let C be a convex body in R^n x R^d, d>=1, with positive mixed
d-volume mu(C)=M. Let P be its finite set of positive d-volume integer
fibers K_z. Suppose H_i={ell_i>=b_i}, i=1,...,m, cover C intersect
(Z^n x R^d), have common mixed mass B>0, and are genuinely active
at global deepest points, whose raw depth is B. Normalize

    ell_i(z,x)=c_i.z+u_i.x,       |u_i|=1.

All caps are nonvertical. Their continuous normal normalization only
rescales their thresholds and does not alter any cap. Positive-depth
points are interior to positive fibers, and an active cap has a proper
section at its anchor, as established in
critical-cap-cover-and-volume-variation.md.

Every global deepest point y satisfies ell_i(y)<=b_i for EVERY i.
Indeed a strict positive margin would allow a small threshold increase
retaining y and deleting a positive slab at the cap's original proper
anchor section, contradicting the depth B at y.

Put F_i(t)=mu(C intersect {ell_i>=t}). This is continuous, since a
nonvertical boundary has zero d-volume in each of the finitely many
fibers. It decreases strictly just to the right of b_i, but need NOT
decrease strictly everywhere: disjoint projection intervals of fibers
can create plateaus. Thus continuity of F_i alone must not be cited as
continuity of its inverse.

For 0<a<B choose the rightmost solution t_i(a)>=b_i of

    F_i(t_i(a))=B-a.                                    (1)

Equivalently, take the supremum of {t:F_i(t)>=B-a}. This supremum is
finite, attained, and satisfies (1). It is nondecreasing in a. Define
t_i(0)=b_i, and take t_i(B)=max_C ell_i, so the endpoint body is
exactly C. Different choices within a plateau change no mixed volume.
Set

    C_a=C intersect intersection_i {ell_i<=t_i(a)},
    M(a)=mu(C_a).                                       (2)

Every C_a is an actual compact convex set. For a>0, all inequalities
in (2) are strict at every original deepest point, because t_i(a)>b_i.
A small relative ball in its original positive fiber survives. Also,
interior points of C approach that point, so C_a has ambient nonempty
interior. Thus C_a is a convex body, M(a)>0, and its relevant intrinsic
dimension remains d. Every original deepest point is still an actual
mixed-integer point of C_a; no rounded or averaged center is introduced.

Each original cap captures at most a in C_a: its retained band in C
has measure exactly a. These same caps still cover all of C_a intersect
Lambda, including all boundary-only fibers. Therefore

    max depth(C_a intersect Lambda)<=a/M(a).             (3)

This bound need not be attained by any of the old caps after trimming.

## 2. Exact mass continuity, occupied parities, and the zero-mass core

For 0<=a<b<=B, the added set C_b minus C_a is contained in the union
of m original bands t_i(a)<ell_i<=t_i(b). Each has mixed mass b-a.
Endpoint choices which add only original measure-zero slabs have no
effect. Hence

    0<=M(b)-M(a)<=m(b-a).                                (4)

The same bound holds for each individual fiber mass. Consequently M
and every fiber mass are Lipschitz and absolutely continuous. This
does not require Hausdorff continuity of C_a through a quantile gap.

At a=0, a point of C_0 in the mixed set belongs to an original covering
cap and also to all opposite weak inequalities. It therefore lies on
at least one cap boundary. Those boundaries are mixed d-volume null,
so

    M(0)=0,       M(B)=M.                                (5)

Every integer section of C_0 has zero d-volume; in particular its
ambient interior is lattice-free in the mixed sense. C_0 can still
contain the original deepest points and nonempty lower-dimensional
fibers. The intrinsic measure at a=0 may change dimension and is NOT
used as a continuation of the positive-d-volume depth in (3).

Write P(a)={z:vol_d((C_a)_z)>0}. No positive fiber can arise outside
the original P, because the deformation is inward. As a INCREASES,
P(a) expands. It is lattice-complete: any integer convex combination
of its bases contains the corresponding Minkowski combination of
positive full-dimensional fibers and therefore has positive volume.
It includes all original deepest bases for every a>0. Its occupied
parity count is nondecreasing in a, bounded above by that of P, and
bounded below by that of the original deepest bases.

Each original positive base has a single entry threshold a_z<B.
At a_z its volume is zero, by continuity; it is positive for a>a_z.
Thus positive bases and occupied parity classes can change only at
finitely many parameter values, even when C is not a polytope. For
decreasing a these events are collapses, not births of new bases.

## 3. A common-rank representation and an overlap identity

On the original mixed source define the nonnegative cap-rank variable

    R_i(w)=(B-F_i(ell_i(w)))_+.

The pushforward of mixed volume under ell_i has no atoms. The ordinary
continuous distribution-transform identity, or directly (1), gives

    mu{R_i>a}=B-a,             0<a<B.                    (6)

Its atom at zero has mass M-B. Up to a null set, membership in the
retained halfspace ell_i<=t_i(a) is exactly R_i<=a. Therefore

    M(a)=mu{max_i R_i<=a}.                               (7)

For completeness, possible quantile plateaus cause no loss in (6)--(7):
their open slabs have zero original measure, and their endpoints are
nonvertical null hyperplanes. The threshold tail computed in (1)
therefore has exactly the same measure as the rank tail. This proves
the identities at every a, not only almost every a.

Thus the deformation is the distribution of the MAXIMUM of ranks
having identical positive-tail marginals. The joint distribution is
the one induced by the actual ambient cap functionals on C; it is not
replaced by independent ranks or an arbitrary coupling.

Let N_a(w)=#{i:ell_i(w)>t_i(a)} and define the excess multiplicity

    E(a)=integral (N_a(w)-1)_+ dmu(w).

Each removed distal cap has mass B-a. Counting its union exactly gives

    M(a)=M-m(B-a)+E(a),
    E(0)=mB-M,
    M(a)=ma-[E(0)-E(a)].                                (8)

E is nonnegative and nonincreasing in a, with E(B)=0. Formula (8)
retains the actual overlap of the moving distal pieces. Monotonicity
of E alone gives no sign for the derivative of M(a)/a; that derivative
depends on the rate of overlap release, not just its total amount.

## 4. Piecewise exact first and second variations for polytopes

Assume now C is a polytope. The original tail functions F_i are
piecewise polynomials of degree at most d: each fiber is a fixed
polytope sliced by one moving plane with fixed normal. On every open
piece with positive section slope, set

    S_i(t)=-F_i'(t)>0.

The slope is the sum of the original proper section (d-1)-areas
over z in P, because the continuous normal has unit length.
Originally zero d-volume fibers do not contribute to this derivative.
The inverse branch is
analytic and algebraic, and

    t_i'(a)=1/S_i(t_i(a)),
    t_i''(a)=-S_i'(t_i(a))/S_i(t_i(a))^3.               (9)

There are only finitely many original breakpoints and quantile-gap
levels. No derivative of an inverse across a gap is asserted.

For independent threshold coordinates T=(T_1,...,T_m), put

    G(T)=mu(C intersect intersection_i {ell_i<=T_i}).

This is a continuous piecewise polynomial of degree at most d on a
finite polyhedral subdivision of threshold space. One direct proof
lists all candidate vertices of each fiber: every intersection of d
independent fixed normals is affine in T. Its feasibility slacks are
affine in T, so finitely many affine walls determine the face
incidences. On each resulting chamber, a fixed triangulation computes
volume by determinants of affine vertex differences, hence a polynomial
of degree at most d. Degenerate chamber faces receive the continuous
restrictions of neighboring volume polynomials.

The analytic algebraic quantile path crosses these finitely many walls
only finitely often unless it lies in a wall identically on a branch.
Indeed a nonzero algebraic function of a has only finitely many zeros
on a bounded branch: choose its polynomial relation with nonzero
constant term after removing a possible identically-zero factor; each
zero then is a zero of that nonzero univariate constant term.
Identically vanishing walls are retained as chamber faces. Thus a
finite subdivision of (0,B) makes M(a)=G(t(a)) analytic on every open
interval, using one chamber polynomial P there (or its restriction
to a persistent chamber face).

Writing P_i and P_ij for that polynomial's derivatives, the exact
chain rule yields

    M'(a)=sum_i P_i/S_i,
    M''(a)=sum_(i,j) P_ij/(S_i S_j)
                  -sum_i P_i S_i'/S_i^3.               (10)

All slopes are evaluated at their corresponding original thresholds.
These are identities, not sign estimates. At parameter knots one
uses the distinct one-sided derivatives; they can differ. Persistent
coincidences do not justify summing a duplicated facet twice: use a
single polynomial restriction as above. On a chamber without such
coincidences, P_i is exactly the exposed moving-facet area left on
the truncated fibers, so the first formula is the familiar exposed
area divided by original section area. In that case 0<=P_i<=S_i,
consistent with the global bound 0<=M'<=m from (4).

## 5. The exact small-parameter creation order

Still in the polytopal case, let

    q_0=max{dim aff((C_0)_z): z in P, (C_0)_z nonempty}.

Only ORIGINALLY POSITIVE fibers occur in this definition. At least
one such core section is nonempty, because it contains an original
deepest point. By (5), 0<=q_0<=d-1. There is a constant c>0 such that

    M(a)=c a^(d-q_0)+O(a^(d-q_0+1))  as a down to0.      (11)

Here is a proof of both the order and the existence of the expansion.
Each active original cap has a proper own-fiber section, so the right
slope S_i(b_i+) is finite and strictly positive. Its right polynomial
tail branch has an analytic inverse near zero, with
t_i(a)=b_i+kappa_i a+O(a^2), kappa_i>0. The finite parametric-volume
description in Section 4 then makes M analytic from the right near
zero, even if the path stays on chamber walls.

Fix a nonempty core section L=(C_0)_z of dimension k at a base in P.
Every candidate vertex of (C_a)_z that persists near zero has an
analytic location x(a)=x(0)+O(a), and x(0) lies in L. Thus
(C_a)_z is contained in L+O(a) times the unit ball, and its d-volume
is O(a^(d-k)). For a lower bound choose a relative k-ball inside L
and an ordinary d-ball B_* inside the original positive K_z. For
epsilon=c_0 a with sufficiently small fixed c_0>0,

    (1-epsilon)L+epsilon B_* subset (C_a)_z.

Convexity gives containment in K_z. Each cap inequality follows from
ell_i<=b_i on L, bounded ell_i on B_*, and the positive linear
threshold increment kappa_i a. This Minkowski combination contains
a fixed-size k-dimensional relative ball thickened in all transverse
directions by a positive multiple of a, so its d-volume is at least
a positive multiple of a^(d-k). Empty core sections at bases in P
remain empty for sufficiently small a, by compactness and the fact
that t_i(a) tends to b_i.

The finitely many fiber bounds show M(a) is bounded above and below
by positive multiples of a^(d-q_0). Its right analytic expansion
therefore has exactly that first nonzero power, proving (11).
This implies M(a)/a tends to0 if q_0<=d-2 and to c if q_0=d-1.
It is an exact core-codimension invariant, not a global monotonicity
claim or a lower bound on c by the desired OC constant.

## 6. Exact counterexample to the proposed universal potentials

Take n=d=1 and the actual full-dimensional hexagonal body

    C={ (z,x): |z|<=1, |x|<=3/2-|z|/2 }.

Its three integer fibers have radii 1,3/2,1 at z=-1,0,1, so M=7.
Every fiber has mass strictly less than M/2: the masses are 2,3,2.
The source is centrally symmetric, and its unique deepest point is
(0,0), with raw depth B=7/2 and normalized depth 1/2. Indeed every
nonvertical through-origin cap has exactly half the mass by symmetry
and null boundaries; closed vertical caps through it have at least
half. Endpoint bases have depth at most their entire own mass 2,
using the isolating vertical halfspace. At base0, any x!=0 lies
strictly inside one horizontal half-mass cap, which can be moved
through it to remove a positive slab. Thus there are no other maxima.

Use these THREE original active caps:

    H_1={x+(5/4)z>=0},
    H_2={x-(5/4)z>=0},
    H_3={-x>=0}.                                       (12)

Each has mass B and is genuinely active at the unique deepest point.
Their normals have the positive relation L_1+L_2+2L_3=0, so they
cover the whole ambient plane. The cover is irredundant even on S:
(1,1/2), (-1,1/2), and (0,-1/2) each belong to exactly one of the
three caps, respectively. Every deepest point is on every cap plane.
The continuous-normal span is one, as d=1 here.

Put k=5/4. Symmetry makes the first two quantiles equal to t(a), and
write the third as s(a). Direct original band volumes give

    t(a)=a                         for 0<=a<=1/4,
         (a+1/4)/2                 for 1/4<=a<=11/4,
         a-5/4                     for 11/4<=a<=7/2;

    s(a)=a/3                       for 0<=a<=3,
         a-2                       for 3<=a<=7/2.        (13)

For example the first original cap's projected positive intervals
are [0,3/2] from the middle fiber and [1/4,9/4] from the upper fiber,
both with unit density. Its band mass up to t is
min(t,3/2)+min(max(t-1/4,0),2). The other endpoint fiber contributes
nothing to this positive band. For H_3 the band mass is
min(s,3/2)+2 min(s,1). Inverting these expressions proves (13).

The actual simultaneous remainder satisfies

    -s(a)<=x<=t(a)-(5/4)|z|,

in addition to the original body constraints. Its middle fiber
has length s+min(3/2,t), and each endpoint fiber has length

    [t-5/4+min(1,s)]_+.

Consequently its exact mixed mass is

    M(a)=4a/3                      for 0<=a<=1/4,
         5a/6+1/8                  for 1/4<=a<=27/20,
         5a/2-17/8                 for 27/20<=a<=11/4,
         3a-7/2                    for 11/4<=a<=7/2.     (14)

All endpoints match. The additional quantile knot a=3 in (13)
cancels in the total mass and is not a missing chamber in (14).
At a=27/20 the endpoint fibers first appear as singletons, and have
positive length immediately afterward. Thus P(a) changes from {0}
to {-1,0,1}; its occupied parity count changes from1 to2.

At this positive parameter, M=5/4 while M' jumps from5/6 to5/2.
Therefore log M has an upward derivative jump, as does M^p for
EVERY real p>0. Neither log concavity nor any positive-power
concavity holds universally. At a=1/4, M' instead drops from4/3
to5/6, so M is not convex either.

The failure of concavity is not confined to a positive-fiber birth.
At a=11/4 the mass is19/4 and its derivative jumps from5/2 to3.
All THREE original fibers have strictly positive length on both
sides of this knot, so the positive base set and its occupied
parities are constant there. Log concavity and every positive-power
concavity also fail locally in this fixed-positive-base regime.

Moreover M(a)/a is constant4/3 initially, strictly decreases on
(1/4,27/20), and strictly increases on (27/20,7/2). Its minimum is
25/27 and its endpoint value is M/B=2. Thus monotonicity in EITHER
direction is false. The actual cover, nonvertical quantiles,
global activity, full body, and no-heavy-fiber condition all hold.

This example is ABOVE the OC threshold. It does not refute a sign
theorem that uses a below-target hypothesis or a further full-rank
condition in higher continuous dimension.

## 7. Continuous-product extension and its precise limitation

For any d>=2 take a centrally symmetric (d-1)-dimensional convex
body L of volume1, and replace C by C x L, using the same three
caps with zero normal in the extra coordinates. Its actual mixed
mass remains7, its fibers have volumes2,3,2, and the same formula
(14) holds with the d-dimensional fiber volume. Central symmetry
and null nonvertical boundaries give depth1/2 at the product origin;
the opposite horizontal caps bound the global maximum by1/2.
The three chosen caps remain genuinely active, nonvertical, and
irredundant. For general volume |L|, scale both a and M by |L|.

Thus the failed potentials are not peculiar to one-dimensional
Hausdorff measure. In this extension their continuous normals still
have rank ONE. No counterexample to a higher-rank or below-target
conditional descent statement is claimed. If a condition about
every deepest point is desired in the product case, it holds as
well: the same horizontal cap displacement first forces x=0 at
any deepest point, and endpoint bases are excluded by their mass2;
then all three margins in (12) vanish regardless of the extra
continuous coordinate.

Exact verifier: verify_coupled_distal_quantile_potential_obstruction_coherent.py.

## 8. Binary padding preserves genuine activity in every integer dimension

The same obstruction extends to every n>=1 and d>=1. Use the original
integer coordinate z and n-1 additional integer coordinates b, and take

    C^(n,d)=C x [0,1]^(n-1) x L,

where L is the volume-one centrally symmetric continuous factor from
Section 7 (omit it when d=1). For v in {0,1}^(n-1), define the affine
function

    D_v(b)=sum_j [v_j+(1-2v_j)b_j].

At binary bases this is the Hamming distance to v. Replace the three
caps (12) by the three caps for EACH v with margins

    ell_(i,v)(z,b,x,w)=ell_i(z,x)-4 D_v(b).             (15)

At b=v these are the original caps. At every other binary base,
ell_(i,v)<0 throughout the fiber family, since the largest original
margin is at most9/4<4. Thus each cap has raw mass B=7/2, captures
only its own binary copy, and all these caps cover the actual mixed
set. They remain irredundant by using the original three uniquely
covered points in each binary copy.

The raw maximum depth is exactly B. At every point (z=0,b=v,x=0,w=0),
any containing halfspace captures at least B from its own binary copy
by the centrally symmetric lower bound of Sections 6--7; other copies
add nonnegative mass. The cap cover gives the matching global upper
bound. Every global deepest point has z=0 and x=0: an endpoint z=+-1
can be isolated with its binary copy by an integer exposing halfspace
and has depth at most its entire fiber mass2; at z=0 a nonzero x is
strictly inside a copy-isolating horizontal half-mass cap, which can
be moved to lose positive mass. Consequently deepest points lie on
the three cap planes of their own copy and strictly below all cap
planes of other copies. All hypotheses concerning global activity
and nonpositive deepest-point margins remain true.

The distal thresholds for (15) are exactly the original t,t,s:
the original outer tails contain only the corresponding binary copy.
Moreover a cut from another copy is automatically satisfied on a
given integer copy, since its margin is negative while t,s>=0.
Thus the one actual intersection body has, at EVERY integer base,
exactly the earlier truncated fibers in each copy. Its total mass is
2^(n-1) times (14); the same concavity and monotonicity failures hold.
This is a global intersection by ambient halfspaces, not independent
fiber editing followed by an unverified convexification.

The total original mass is M_n=7*2^(n-1), while individual fiber
volumes are2,3,2. Hence every fiber is strictly lighter than

    M_n/2^n=7/2.

The normalized maximum depth is B/M_n=2^(-n), which remains ABOVE
the target gamma_d 2^(-n). In d>1 the continuous cap-normal rank is
still one. These explicit limitations continue to distinguish the
example from a below-target or higher-rank conditional obstruction.
